text.p: Investors in the gold market who had bet on the metal plunging to fresh lows in the near future had their dreams shattered on Friday by the dollar's weakness.

In other commodity markets base metals remained volatile with Thursday's warning shot from London Metal Exchange (LME) authorities having little immediate impact on liquidity problems in zinc and aluminium markets.

Tightness in zinc hit the premium for cash metal, which zoomed up by more than 50 percent on Friday, and the spread in aluminium also held at strong levels. The movements occurred despite a warning by the LME on Thursday about players with dominant positions pushing prices higher.
The strength of the spreads helped to stabilise three months prices, which had corrected lower in the morning from heady levels the previous evening.

In zinc, players scrambled in the afternoon ring and bid up the cash/threes spread, which ballooned to a $155 backwardation from $100 on Thursday. One trader said it appeared to be a liquidity problem after cash metal was bid up during the morning but another said renewed rumours of personnel changes in the Chinese metals industry may have triggered speculative moves.

An official at China's Zhuzhou zinc smelter on Tuesday denied rumours of sackings following big losses on global metals markets. Chinese smelters last year sold forward at low prices as much as 250,000 tonnes, and most of the positions mature in September.
On the LME on Friday, the bulk of the tightness was in the September/August spread, at a $90 backwardation. Three months zinc took a back seat, ending $7 firmer at $1,547.

Aluminium found renewed buying interest after correcting lower in the morning to a low of $1,732."I think the market needed that.., it confirmed support down there," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis. Three months ended the day with pared losses at $1,746, down $16.50.

Next week should see more of the same, said Bahr. "Any weakness will be taken as an opportunity to establish or re-establish long positions," he said. Tightness kept bubbling under the market, with the cash/threes ending at a $15/$20 backwardation, little changed from Thursday's $20.

Copper slipped in the afternoon after fund selling on Comex triggered stops, hitting a low of $2,284. But the market found good base support and stabilised, ending the day $45 lower at $2,288. A stocks increase of 2,925 tonnes reminded the market of rising inventories and a looming surplus.

Speculative selling on nickel forced prices to a low of $7,010, a long-term support level, but prices edged higher by the close to end $175 softer at $7,085. "Once nickel starts slipping, the momentum can take it lower...If the specs keep hunting for stops, they might trigger some under $7,000," Bahr said.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals ended solidly higher Friday, as gold in particular benefited from the sharp slide in the U.S. dollar, U.S. treasury bonds and U.S. stocks. "The gold market was looking for a reason to recover after seeing 12-year lows last month and the sell off in financial markets provided the impetus," Chase Manhattan managing director for global commodities, Dinsa Mehta, said. "The weakness in the dollar was especially significant as the dollar's strength has been a factor in gold's weakness of late," he said. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $326.90/40 an ounce, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $323.70 and the New York close around $321.70/20.

Mounting concerns about potential declines in production in some areas and quality in other parts of the world due to harsh weather boosted CBOT wheat futures to a higher close, traders said. "We keep hearing more about Canada's crop shrinking, problems in Australia and in Europe with the rains and flooding there are concerns about quality," said Dave Armstrong, analyst for ABN Amro, The Chicago Corp. Wheat found support at the end of the week on a Canadian Wheat Board outlook for a wheat corp in western Canada this year of 21.6 million tonnes, below the 29.5 million produced last year. CBOT soft red winter wheat closed one to six cents per bushel higher, with September up four at $3.67-1/4. Traders said a recovery in corn futures and a late rally in soybeans helped boost wheat futures.

NYMEX crude ended the week in the red after the market was dealt a one-two punch by sharp losses in gasoline prices and news that Iraqi oil exports will restart next week. "There was just a bloodbath in the gasoline market, and the Iraqi news just added to it," said a New York crude trader. September crude settled 55 cents down at $19.54 a barrel, netting a 76 cent loss for the week. September gasoline ended off 2.34 cents a gallon at 61.99 cents and September heating oil finished 1.01 cents lower at 54.29 cents a gallon.
